column9: Which piece of glassware gives the most precise volume measurement of a liquid?

column16: Erlenmeyer flask

column29: Which tool has the most lines (markings) packed close together?

column9: Which tool should you use to pick up a hot beaker?
column15: Beaker tongs
column16: Watch glass
column28: Beaker tongs are made to grip a hot beaker. A test tube holder only fits test tubes, a watch glass is a lid, and a spatula scoops solids.
column29: Which tool is made to grip something large and hot, not small like a test tube?

column9: The part of a lab report that holds your graphs and possible calculations is the ___ section.
column28: Analysis = graphs and possible calculations. It comes after Observations (data tables) and before the Conclusion.
column29: It is the section where you work with your data after you record it.

column9: Once the experiment is over, you can take your goggles off while you clean up.

column29: Can a chemical still splash while you are washing glassware?

column9: A classmate's sleeve catches on fire during a lab. What safety equipment is used on a person who is on fire?
column15: Fire extinguisher
column16: Fire blanket
column28: A fire blanket is used when a person is on fire; it smothers the flames. A fire extinguisher (PASS) is for a fire on the bench or floor, not sprayed on a person.
column29: Which item smothers flames by wrapping around someone?

column9: Which variable goes on the x-axis of a graph?
column15: Constant
column16: Confounding variable
column28: The independent variable (what you change) goes on the x-axis; the dependent variable (what you measure) goes on the y-axis.
column29: Think about which variable you set first, before you measure anything.

column9: Match each lab tool to the property it measures.
column15: Digital scale :: Mass
column16: Thermometer :: Temperature
column28: Graduated cylinder: volume (mL). Digital scale: mass (g). Thermometer: temperature (°C). Meter stick: length (mm, cm, m). Stopwatch: time (s).
column29: Think of the unit each tool reads: mL, g, °C, cm, or s.

column9: A hypothesis is just a guess.
column28: False. A hypothesis is a testable explanation or prediction based on prior life experiences, written If... then... because.... A guess has no reason behind it.
column29: What does the "because" part of a hypothesis add?

column9: Which variable is measured during the procedure to see the effect of the variable the experimenter sets?
column15: Independent variable
column16: Constant
column28: The dependent variable depends on the independent variable and is measured during the procedure. It is "what was measured."
column29: Is it the one you change, or the one you record?

column9: Which heat source changes electrical energy into thermal energy and has no open flame?
column15: Hot plate
column16: Ring stand
column28: A hot plate plugs in and changes electrical energy to thermal energy. A Bunsen burner uses gas (chemical to thermal) and makes an open flame; a ring stand and wire gauze only hold things.
column29: Which one plugs into the wall?

column9: To use a fire extinguisher, remember PASS: Pull, Aim, ___, Sweep.
column28: PASS = Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, Sweep side to side.
column29: After you aim the hose, what do you do to the handle?

column9: Which tool is used to scoop small amounts of a solid chemical?
column15: Funnel
column16: Spatula
column28: A spatula scoops solids. A pipette moves small amounts of liquid, a funnel pours liquids into narrow openings, and a stirring rod mixes.
column29: Two of these tools are only for liquids. Which one is for powders and crystals?

column9: Which part of a lab report gives step-by-step directions for the experiment?
column15: Observations
column16: Conclusion
column28: The procedure is the step-by-step directions, so anyone could repeat the experiment.
column29: Which part reads like a recipe?

column9: Hot glass looks different from cold glass, so you can tell by looking when a beaker is safe to touch.
column28: False. Hot glass looks just like cold glass. Use beaker tongs or let it cool; never judge by looking.
column29: Picture a beaker that just came off the hot plate. Does it glow or change color?

column9: Which question can NOT be answered with a scientific experiment?
column15: Does salt change the temperature at which water boils?
column16: Do plants grow taller with more light?
column17: Does a heavier ball roll farther down a ramp?
column28: Science cannot test opinions and values. "Good" is an opinion, so there is nothing to measure. The other questions have something you can change and something you can measure.
column29: For each question, ask: what would I measure?

column9: Put the steps of the scientific method in order.
column15: Analyze data
column16: State the problem
column28: State the problem, research and gather information, form a hypothesis, test the hypothesis, analyze data, draw conclusions.
column29: You need a question before you can research it, and you need data before you can analyze it.

column9: Put the parts of a lab report in order.
column15: Conclusion
column16: Hypothesis
column28: Problem, Hypothesis, Procedure, Observations, Analysis, Conclusion. It follows the same order you work in during a lab.
column29: Start with why you are experimenting and end with the summary.

column9: Maya puts bean plants under lamps for 2, 4, 6, and 8 hours a day and measures their height after 3 weeks. What is the independent variable?
column15: Hours of light each day
column16: Type of bean plant
column28: The independent variable is set by the experimenter. Maya chose 2, 4, 6, and 8 hours of light. Height is what she measures (dependent).
column29: Which variable did Maya change on purpose?

column9: Jae drops a sugar cube into water at 10 °C, 30 °C, 50 °C, and 70 °C and times how long it takes to dissolve. What is the dependent variable?
column15: Size of the sugar cube
column16: Time for the sugar to dissolve
column28: The dependent variable is what was measured: the time to dissolve, in seconds. Jae set the water temperature, so that is the independent variable.
column29: What is Jae recording with the stopwatch?

column9: Group A is testing whether the amount of salt in water changes how long the water takes to freeze. Which hypothesis is written in the correct format?
column14: If more salt is added to water, then it will take longer to freeze.
column15: Does adding more salt to water change how long it takes to freeze?
column16: Salt water is better than plain water, so it will take longer to freeze.
column17: If more salt is added to water, then it will take longer to freeze, because salt gets in the way of water freezing.
column28: A hypothesis has all three parts: If (the IV change)... then (the DV prediction)... because (a reason from what you already know). One choice is missing the because, one is a question, and one is an opinion.
column29: Count the parts. A complete hypothesis has three key words.

column9: A data table has two columns: Water Depth (m) and Temperature (°C). The students chose the depths and measured the temperature at each one. What is the correct graph title?
column15: Water Depth vs. Temperature
column16: Water Depth and Temperature
column28: The title format is "DV vs. IV." Temperature was measured (DV) and depth was chosen (IV), so the title is Temperature vs. Water Depth.
column29: The title format is ___ vs. ___. Which variable was measured, and which was chosen?

column9: Group C drops a ball from heights of 50 cm, 100 cm, and 150 cm and measures how high it bounces. What should the FIRST column of their data table be?
column15: Drop height (cm)
column16: Type of ball
column28: The independent variable is always first in a data table. Group C chose the drop heights, so Drop height (cm) goes first and Bounce height (cm) comes after it.
column29: Which variable did Group C choose before they measured anything?

column9: In Maya's plant experiment, every plant gets the same pot size, the same soil, and 50 mL of water each day. What are these?
column15: Dependent variables
column16: Constants
column28: Constants remain the same during an experiment to obtain reliable data. Keeping pot, soil, and water the same means only the light changes.
column29: Did these things change, or stay the same, from plant to plant?

column9: Jae tests whether fertilizer helps grass grow. Four trays of grass get 0 g, 5 g, 10 g, and 15 g of fertilizer. Which tray is the control group?
column14: The tray with 15 g of fertilizer
column15: The tray with 5 g of fertilizer
column16: All four trays together
column17: The tray with 0 g of fertilizer
column28: The control group gets none of the treatment, so it is the baseline. The trays with fertilizer are compared to the 0 g tray.
column29: Which tray shows what grass does with NO fertilizer?

column9: Which is the correct way to read the volume of water in a graduated cylinder?
column14: Get down at eye level and read the bottom of the meniscus
column15: Look down from above and read the top of the meniscus
column16: Hold the cylinder up and tilt it toward the light
column17: Read the top edge of the water where it touches the glass
column28: Always get on eye level and measure from the bottom of the meniscus (the curve of the water). Reading from above or at the edges gives a wrong value.
column29: The water surface curves. Where should your eyes be, and which part of the curve do you read?

column9: What is the main difference between a scientific law and a scientific theory?
column14: A law is a guess; a theory has been proven true forever.
column15: A law describes what happens; a theory explains why it happens.
column16: A theory becomes a law once it gets enough evidence.
column17: A law explains why something happens; a theory only describes it.
column28: A law describes what happens and does not explain why. A theory is an explanation that comes from many investigations and can be modified. A theory does not "grow up" into a law.
column29: One of them answers "what happens?" and the other answers "why?"

column9: Match each term to its meaning.
column14: Independent variable :: Set (changed) by the experimenter
column15: Dependent variable :: Measured during the procedure
column16: Constant :: Kept the same to get reliable data
column17: Control group :: Baseline to compare the experimental data to
column18: Confounding variable :: Environmental factor beyond the experimenter's control
column19: Bias :: Opinion or idea based on beliefs instead of data
column28: Independent = what was changed; dependent = what was measured; constants stay the same; the control group is the baseline; confounding variables are outside factors you can't control; bias is belief instead of data.
column29: Start with the ones you are sure of (changed vs. measured), then match the rest.

column9: Match each piece of lab equipment to its use.
column14: Watch glass :: Lid that prevents splattering
column15: Mortar and pestle :: Grinding solids into powder
column16: Test tube holder :: Holding a test tube while heating it
column17: Funnel :: Pouring liquid into a narrow opening
column18: Wire gauze :: Sits on the iron ring to support a beaker over a flame
column28: Watch glass: lid. Mortar and pestle: grinding. Test tube holder: holds a hot test tube. Funnel: pouring. Wire gauze: rests on the iron ring under a beaker.
column29: Think about what each tool looks like: a shallow dish, a bowl with a club, clamp tongs, a cone, a wire square.

column9: Which of these are correct lab safety rules? Select all that apply.
column14: Waft fumes toward your nose to smell a chemical
column15: Put broken glass in its own broken-glass container
column16: Taste a tiny amount to help identify a chemical
column17: Eat snacks only if they stay on your side of the lab bench
column18: Use the eye wash station if a chemical splashes in your eyes
column19: Point the open end of a heated test tube toward your lab partner
column28: Waft, never taste. Broken glass goes in its own disposal. Use the eye wash for splashes. No eating or drinking in the lab, and always angle a heated test tube away from people.
column29: Check each rule: would it keep chemicals out of your mouth, eyes, and skin?

column9: Which tools can be used to measure the volume of a liquid? Select all that apply.
column15: Digital scale
column16: Graduated cylinder
column28: A beaker, graduated cylinder, and Erlenmeyer flask all have mL markings for volume (the graduated cylinder is the most precise). A scale measures mass, a thermometer temperature, and a meter stick length.
column29: Which tools have mL markings on the side?

column9: Jae places an empty weigh boat on the digital scale. Before he adds any chemical, he must ___ the scale.
column28: Always zero the scale with the weigh boat on it BEFORE you add chemicals. Then the scale shows only the mass of the chemical, not the boat.
column29: What button do you press so the scale reads 0.00 g with the boat on it?

column9: Constants are used as a baseline to compare the experimental data against.
column28: False. That describes the control group. Constants are things kept the same during the experiment to obtain reliable data.
column29: Is a baseline a thing you keep the same, or a group you compare to?

column9: Which part of a lab report is a statement of why you are experimenting and identifies the variables?
column15: Conclusion
column16: Problem
column28: The problem states why you are experimenting and names the variables, for example "How does [IV] affect [DV]?"
column29: Which part asks the question the whole experiment is trying to answer?

column9: Ava needs to add a very precise amount of liquid, exactly 2.0 mL, to a test tube. Which tool is best?
column15: Erlenmeyer flask
column16: Test tube rack
column28: A pipette delivers very precise amounts of liquid. A beaker and flask only give rough volumes, and a rack just holds test tubes.
column29: Which tool is made for very small, very precise amounts?

column9: Which statement is an unbiased observation?
column14: The solution turned blue 30 seconds after the drops were added.
column15: The blue solution looks really pretty.
column16: I think our reaction worked better than everyone else's.
column17: Brand X chemicals always give the best results.
column28: Observations are unbiased statements using your 5 senses and data. Color and time are facts anyone can check; the others are opinions or beliefs.
column29: Which statement would every person in the room agree on, no matter what they believe?

column9: Jae tests whether fertilizer affects plant height. Plant 1 gets no fertilizer and sits in a sunny window. Plant 2 gets 10 g of fertilizer and sits in a dark closet. What is the biggest flaw?
column14: He should have measured the plants in inches.
column15: Light was not kept constant, so two variables changed.
column16: Plant 1 should have gotten fertilizer too.
column17: He did not use a control group.
column28: Only the independent variable (fertilizer) should change. Because light also changed, Jae can't tell whether fertilizer or light caused the difference. Plant 1 is a fine control group.
column29: List everything that was different between the two plants. How many things should differ?

column9: Group B tests how ramp height affects how far a toy car rolls. They use a red car for the 10 cm and 20 cm trials, but a bigger blue car for the 30 cm trial. Which variable was NOT held constant?
column15: The distance the car rolls
column16: The car used
column28: Ramp height is supposed to change (IV) and distance is measured (DV). The car should be a constant, but it changed in the 30 cm trial, so that result can't be compared fairly.
column29: Which thing changed that was NOT supposed to change?

column9: Maya tests whether chewing gum affects how fast students solve a 20-problem math sheet. Group 1 chews mint gum while solving. What should the control group do?
column14: Chew two pieces of mint gum while solving the sheet
column15: Chew gum while solving a different, easier math sheet
column16: Skip the math sheet and just chew gum
column17: Solve the same math sheet in the same room without chewing gum
column28: The control group gets no treatment (no gum) but everything else stays the same: same sheet, same room. Then it is a baseline to compare the gum group to.
column29: The control group skips only the thing being tested. What should stay exactly the same?

column9: Jae's data: water at 10 °C took 95 s to dissolve a sugar cube, 30 °C took 60 s, 50 °C took 32 s, and 70 °C took 15 s. Which conclusion does the data support?
column14: As water temperature increases, the time to dissolve decreases.
column15: As water temperature increases, the time to dissolve increases.
column16: Water temperature has no effect on dissolving time.
column17: Sugar dissolves fastest in the coldest water.
column28: As temperature goes up (10 to 70 °C), the time goes down (95 to 15 s). That is an inverse relationship: hotter water dissolves sugar faster.
column29: Follow the numbers: when temperature goes up, does the time go up or down?

column9: Group E measured how far a paper airplane flew with 1, 2, 3, and 4 paper clips on its nose: 6.2 m, 5.1 m, 4.0 m, and 2.9 m. A student says, "Our data proves an airplane with 8 paper clips would fly 0 m." Does the data support this claim?
column14: Yes. The distance drops about 1.1 m for each clip, so it must reach 0 m.
column15: No. They never tested 8 paper clips, so the data cannot show what would happen.
column16: Yes. More paper clips always means a shorter flight.
column17: No. The airplane would fly farther with 8 paper clips.
column28: A conclusion should only use the data collected. The group tested 1 to 4 clips, so a claim about 8 clips needs more testing; the pattern could change.
column29: What range of paper clips did the group actually test?

column9: Leo tests whether music helps plants grow. He plays music for one plant and keeps one plant in silence, then measures them once after a week. The music plant is 1 cm taller. What is the best way to make his results more reliable?
column14: Play the music louder for the music plant
column15: Only measure the music plant
column16: Use many plants in each group and repeat the trials
column17: Change the type of plant in the silent group
column28: With one plant per group, the 1 cm difference could be chance. More plants and repeated trials make the results reliable. Changing the plant type would add a second variable.
column29: Could one plant just happen to be a little taller? How do scientists make sure a result wasn't luck?

column9: Maya tests how the amount of water (25 mL, 50 mL, or 75 mL per day) affects the height of radish plants after 2 weeks. Which should be kept CONSTANT? Select all that apply.
column15: Amount of sunlight
column16: Type of soil
column28: Seed type, sunlight, soil, and pot size must stay the same so only water changes. Water amount is the independent variable and plant height is the dependent variable, so they are not constants.
column29: First find the IV and DV. Everything else that could affect height should stay the same.

column9: Put the steps in order for measuring the mass of salt with a digital scale.
column14: Add salt to the weigh boat with a spatula
column15: Turn on the digital scale
column16: Record the mass in grams
column18: Place an empty weigh boat on the scale
column28: Turn on the scale, place the empty weigh boat on it, zero the scale, add salt with the spatula, then record the mass in g. Zeroing before adding salt means the reading is only the salt.
column29: The scale must read 0.00 g with the boat on it before any chemical goes in.

column9: Group D's hypothesis: "If the mass of a pendulum increases, then the time for one swing will stay the same, because gravity pulls on all masses the same way." How should they set up their graph?
column14: x-axis: Time per swing (s); y-axis: Mass (g); title: Mass vs. Time per Swing
column15: x-axis: Mass (g); y-axis: Time per swing (s); title: Mass vs. Time per Swing
column16: x-axis: Time per swing (s); y-axis: Mass (g); title: Time per Swing vs. Mass
column17: x-axis: Mass (g); y-axis: Time per swing (s); title: Time per Swing vs. Mass
column28: The "If" part names the IV (mass), which goes on the x-axis. The "then" part names the DV (time per swing), which goes on the y-axis. The title is DV vs. IV: Time per Swing vs. Mass.
column29: Find the IV in the "If" part and the DV in the "then" part. Then use the axis and title rules.

column9: If the data does not support the hypothesis, the experiment failed and the data should be thrown out.
column28: False. Data that does not support the hypothesis is still a valid result. The conclusion explains the results and possible error, and the scientist may revise the hypothesis and test again.
column29: Can scientists learn something from a prediction that turned out wrong?

column9: Group A tests how the amount of salt affects how fast ice melts on the sidewalk outside. Halfway through, the sun comes out from behind the clouds. The sunlight is best described as a
column15: control group
column16: dependent variable
column28: Confounding variables are environmental factors beyond the experimenter's control. Group A did not choose the sunlight, but it can change how fast the ice melts.
column29: Did Group A choose the sunlight, measure it, or have no control over it?

column9: Ava works for a company that sells Brand Z fertilizer. In her report she only includes the trials where Brand Z plants grew the tallest and leaves out the others. What is the problem?
column14: Confounding variable: the weather changed during the trials
column15: Bias: her beliefs are deciding which data she reports
column16: No independent variable: she did not change anything
column17: No constants: she used different plants
column28: Bias is an opinion or idea based on beliefs instead of data. Leaving out data that doesn't match what you want is biased; all trials must be reported.
column29: Is the problem with the experiment itself, or with how Ava chose what to report?

column9: Group D drops a tennis ball from different heights and measures how high it bounces. Which hypothesis correctly matches their experiment?
column14: If the bounce height increases, then the drop height will increase, because the ball has more energy.
column15: If the drop height increases, then the bounce height will increase.
column16: If the drop height increases, then the bounce height will increase, because the ball gains more energy falling farther.
column17: If a tennis ball is used, then it will be the most fun to bounce, because tennis is a great sport.
column28: The "If" part should name the IV (drop height, which Group D chooses) and the "then" part the DV (bounce height, which they measure), plus a because. One choice has the variables backwards, one has no because, and one is an opinion.
column29: Which variable did Group D choose? That one belongs in the "If" part.

column9: Group C's whole conclusion is: "Our hypothesis was supported." Based on what a conclusion should include, what is missing?
column14: A list of the lab equipment used
column15: The step-by-step directions
column16: A new data table with all the measurements
column17: A summary of the analysis, possible sources of error, and an explanation of the results
column28: A conclusion is a summary of the analysis, the proposed error, and an explanation of the results. Equipment and steps belong in the procedure, and data tables belong in observations.
column29: What three things does a conclusion summarize or explain?

column9: Group E drops paper helicopters with wings 4 cm, 6 cm, and 8 cm long from the same height and times each fall. Which problem statement fits their experiment?

column15: How does the fall time affect the wing length of a paper helicopter?
column16: What is the effect of drop height on the fall time of a paper helicopter?
column17: Paper helicopters with longer wings are better.
column28: A problem statement names the IV and DV: How does [IV] affect [DV]? Group E changed wing length (IV) and measured fall time (DV). Drop height was a constant, and the last choice is an opinion, not a question.
column29: Which variable did Group E change on purpose, and which did they time?

column9: Which piece of lab equipment holds several test tubes upright at the same time?
column15: Test tube holder
column16: Ring stand

column29: Look for the tool that works like a stand with a row of holes.

column9: Which tool is used to mix chemicals together to make a solution?
column15: Watch glass
column16: Stirring rod
column28: A stirring rod is used to mix chemicals and create solutions. A funnel helps pour liquids, a watch glass is a lid, and a weigh boat holds a chemical on the scale.
column29: Which tool would you swirl around inside a beaker?

column9: What is the job of a weigh boat?
column14: It holds the chemical being measured and protects the scale
column15: It heats a liquid over a flame
column16: It measures the volume of a liquid
column17: It grinds a solid into a powder
column28: A weigh boat holds the chemical you are measuring and protects the scale from it. It does not heat, measure volume, or grind anything; those jobs belong to a hot plate, a graduated cylinder, and a mortar and pestle.
column29: Think about what sits between the chemical and the top of the digital scale.

column9: Maya needs to add a liquid one drop at a time. Which tool should she use?
column15: Beaker
column16: Spatula
column28: A dropper moves liquids when you need to transfer them drop by drop. A funnel pours from a large container into a smaller one, a beaker holds liquid, and a spatula moves solids.
column29: Which tool lets out a tiny amount of liquid each time you squeeze it?

column9: Which piece of glassware is used for performing small chemical reactions?
column15: Graduated cylinder
column16: Watch glass
column28: A test tube is used for small chemical reactions. A graduated cylinder measures volume, a watch glass is a lid, and a funnel helps pour liquids.
column29: Which one is a small glass tube, often held in a holder while it is heated?

column9: Which piece of glassware has a wide bottom and a narrow neck, and is used for heating liquids but can also measure and hold them?
column15: Test tube
column16: Graduated cylinder
column28: An Erlenmeyer flask is cone-shaped, with a wide bottom and a narrow neck. It is used for heating liquids, and it can also measure and hold them. A beaker has straight sides and a spout.
column29: Picture a container shaped like a cone with a short tube on top.

column9: Which piece of glassware has straight sides and a spout, is used for holding, mixing, heating, and measuring volume, but gives only a rough volume?
column15: Watch glass
column16: Beaker
column28: A beaker is used for holding, mixing, heating, and measuring volume. Its markings are only rough, so use a graduated cylinder when you need a precise volume.
column29: Which container looks like a wide cup with a lip for pouring?

column9: A Bunsen burner is powered by gas. What energy change happens when it heats a beaker?

column16: Chemical energy → thermal energy
column28: A Bunsen burner burns gas, so it changes the chemical energy stored in the gas into thermal energy and makes an open flame. Electrical energy would need a plug, and the burner gives off heat rather than storing it.
column29: Where is the energy stored before the burner is lit?

column9: What should you do before you start any lab?
column14: Turn on the hot plate so it can warm up
column15: Mix a few chemicals to see what happens
column16: Read the lab all the way through
column17: Take off your goggles so you can see better
column28: Read the lab through all the way before doing anything else, so you know every step and safety rule before you touch the equipment.
column29: You can't follow directions you haven't seen yet.

column9: Something goes wrong during a lab, but it seems very minor. What should you do first?
column15: Clean it up quietly so no one notices
column16: Finish the lab and mention it next week
column17: Ask your lab partner to handle it

column29: Who is the adult in charge of safety in the lab?

column9: When should you wear safety goggles in the lab?
column14: Only while you are heating something
column15: Only when the teacher is watching
column16: Only when you are using glassware
column17: Whenever you are using chemicals or fire
column28: Always wear safety goggles whenever you are using chemicals or fire. Splashes can happen at any step, not only while heating, and not only when someone is watching.
column29: Which choice protects your eyes the most often?

column9: Why should long hair be tied back during a lab?
column14: It makes the data table neater
column15: It could catch fire or fall into chemicals
column16: It helps you read the scale
column17: It keeps the goggles from fogging up
column28: Tying hair back (and skipping loose clothing and jewelry) keeps it away from open flames and chemicals. It helps prevent fires and keeps hair out of your experiment.
column29: Think about what could happen when you lean over a Bunsen burner.

column9: Jae has some leftover liquid chemical at the end of a lab. What should he do with it?

column15: Pour it back into the stock bottle
column16: Pour it down the sink right away
column17: Leave it on the lab bench for the next class
column28: Always dispose of chemicals correctly and ask before pouring anything down the sink. Pouring leftovers back into the stock bottle can ruin the whole bottle, and leaving them out is unsafe for the next class.
column29: When in doubt, who should you ask?

column9: Why should you never walk away from a lit Bunsen burner or a plugged-in hot plate?

column15: It will make the thermometer read the wrong temperature
column16: It changes the mass shown on the scale
column17: It makes the meniscus harder to read

column29: What could happen to a paper towel left near a heat source with no one watching?

column9: Which outfit is the safest to wear on a lab day?
column15: A loose sweater with long dangling sleeves
column16: Long pants and closed-toe shoes
column28: Closed-toe shoes and long pants are the safest clothing for lab. They protect your skin from spills and broken glass, and nothing loose can catch on equipment or a flame.
column29: Which outfit covers the most skin and has nothing hanging loose?

column9: Before using a beaker, Leo notices a small crack in it. What should he do?
column14: Use it carefully and hope it holds
column15: Heat it first to see if it breaks
column16: Cover the crack with tape
column17: Tell the teacher and do not use it
column28: Tell the teacher if your glassware is cracked before you use it. Cracked glass can break, especially when it is heated or filled.
column29: Who needs to know about damaged equipment?

column9: Match each piece of safety gear with the way it keeps you safe.
column14: Safety goggles :: Protects your eyes from splashes
column15: Lab apron :: Protects your clothing
column16: Heat-resistant gloves :: Protects your hands from hot objects
column17: Safety shower :: Rinses a chemical off your body
column28: Safety goggles protect your eyes, a lab apron protects your clothing, heat-resistant gloves protect your hands from hot objects, and the safety shower rinses a chemical off your body.
column29: Match each item to the part of you (or your clothes) that it covers or cleans.

column9: In the scientific method, which step comes right after you form a hypothesis?
column15: Test the hypothesis
column16: Draw conclusions
column28: The steps are: state the problem, research and gather information, form a hypothesis, test the hypothesis, analyze data, and draw conclusions. Once you have a prediction, you test it.
column29: Once you have a prediction, what do you need to do to find out if it is right?

column9: Ava tests whether the color of a cup (black, white, or silver) changes how warm the water inside gets after 1 hour in the sun. What is the independent variable?
column15: Amount of water in each cup
column16: Color of the cup
column28: The independent variable is what Ava changes on purpose: the cup color. The water temperature is what she measures (dependent variable), and the amount of water and the time in the sun are constants.
column29: Which thing did Ava choose to make different from cup to cup?

column9: Leo tests how the number of batteries (1, 2, or 3) affects how brightly a bulb glows. He measures the brightness with a light meter. What is the dependent variable?
column15: Number of batteries
column16: Type of bulb
column28: The dependent variable is what Leo measures: the brightness. He sets the number of batteries (independent variable), and the bulb type and wire length should stay the same (constants).
column29: What number does the light meter give him?

column9: Group F tests whether the temperature of water changes how long a fizzing tablet takes to dissolve. Which of these should be a constant?
column15: The time the tablet takes to dissolve
column16: How many bubbles the tablet makes
column17: The amount of water in each cup
column28: A constant stays the same in every trial. Using the same amount of water means only the temperature changes. Water temperature is the independent variable, and dissolving time and bubbles are results that get observed.
column29: Which choice should stay exactly the same from one cup to the next?

column9: Which of these is written in the correct format for a problem statement?
column15: How does the amount of sunlight affect the height of a plant?
column16: If plants get more sunlight, then they will grow taller.
column28: A problem statement is a question that names the variables: How does [IV] affect [DV]? Of the other choices, one is a claim, one is the start of a hypothesis, and one is only a topic.
column29: A problem is a question. Which choice asks one and names what is changed and what is measured?

column9: In which part of a lab report do you record your data tables?
column15: Procedure
column16: Problem
column28: Data tables go in the Observations section, where you record what you measured and saw during the lab. The procedure is the directions, and the problem and hypothesis come before any data.
column29: This part is named for what you see and record while the experiment runs.

column9: Which of these is an example of a scientific model?
column14: A computer simulation of a hurricane
column15: A data table of plant heights
column16: A list of lab safety rules
column28: A model represents an idea, event, or object to help people understand it. A computer simulation is a model: it tests a process and collects data. A data table is data, a rule list is not a model, and a beaker of salt water is a real sample.
column29: Which choice stands in for something too big or too complex to study directly?

column9: The three main categories of science are life science, Earth science, and ___ science.
column28: The three main categories are life science, Earth science, and physical science. Physical science studies matter and energy.
column29: This branch studies matter and energy, like chemistry and physics.

column9: A hypothesis must be ___, meaning you can design an experiment to check whether it is right.
column28: A hypothesis is a testable prediction, written If... then... because.... If no experiment could ever check it, it is not a scientific hypothesis.
column29: Think about what you DO with a hypothesis during an experiment.

column9: In Mr. Erickson's class, how is the title of a graph written?
column15: Dependent variable vs. Independent variable
column16: Hypothesis vs. Conclusion
column28: The title is DV vs. IV: the measured variable first, then the variable you changed. For example: Plant Height vs. Water per Day.
column29: The variable on the y-axis is named first.

column9: Which of these is an example of a confounding variable in an outdoor plant experiment?
column14: The amount of water the experimenter gives each plant
column15: The height of the plants at the end
column16: The type of seed planted in every pot
column17: A surprise hailstorm that damages some of the plants
column28: A confounding variable is an environmental factor beyond the experimenter's control, like a hailstorm. The water is chosen by the experimenter, the height is measured, and the seed type is a constant.
column29: Which choice could the experimenter NOT control?

column9: A scientific theory can be modified when new information becomes available.
column28: True. A theory is an explanation based on many observations and investigations, and it can be changed as scientists learn more. That is one way science improves over time.
column29: Do scientists ever change their explanations when they get new evidence?

column9: In a Bunsen burner setup, what is the job of the ring stand?
column15: It measures the temperature of the liquid
column16: It holds equipment, like the iron ring, above the flame
column17: It stirs the liquid while it heats
column28: A Bunsen burner makes an open flame, so it needs extra equipment to hold things above it. The ring stand holds the iron ring, the wire gauze sits on the ring, and the beaker sits on the gauze.
column29: The ring stand is a tall metal rod with a heavy base. What could it hold up?

column9: Read this hypothesis: "If the temperature of a room increases, then a candle will burn faster, because wax melts more quickly when it is warm." What is the independent variable?
column15: The temperature of the room
column16: The type of wax
column28: The If part names the independent variable: the room temperature, which the experimenter changes. The then part names the dependent variable: how fast the candle burns. Wax type and candle size should be constants.
column29: Look at the If part of the hypothesis.

column9: Leo times how long ice cubes take to melt in cups of water at 10 °C, 20 °C, 30 °C, and 40 °C. What should the x-axis of his graph show?
column15: Size of the ice cube (cm)
column16: Water temperature (°C)
column28: The x-axis shows the independent variable, the one Leo chose: water temperature. Melting time is what he measured, so it goes on the y-axis.
column29: Which variable did Leo pick before any trial started?

column9: Group A heated water and recorded its temperature every minute: 0 min, 20 °C; 1 min, 31 °C; 2 min, 42 °C; 3 min, 52 °C; 4 min, 63 °C. Which statement describes the trend?
column14: As heating time increases, the temperature decreases.
column15: Heating time has no effect on the temperature.
column16: The temperature went up at first, then went down.
column17: As heating time increases, the temperature increases.
column28: Read down both columns: as the time goes up (0 to 4 min), the temperature goes up (20 to 63 °C). Both increase together, so the temperature increases as heating time increases.
column29: When the time gets bigger, does the temperature get bigger or smaller?

column9: Maya hung masses on a spring and measured how far it stretched: 100 g, 2.0 cm; 200 g, 4.1 cm; 300 g, 6.0 cm; 400 g, 8.1 cm. Use the pattern to predict the stretch for a 250 g mass. Answer in cm.
column28: 250 g is halfway between 200 g and 300 g, so the stretch should be about halfway between 4.1 cm and 6.0 cm: about 5.0 cm. This is a fair prediction because 250 g is inside the range of masses Maya actually tested.
column29: Find the two masses on either side of 250 g. The answer is between their stretches.

column9: A lab report says: "Our data supported the hypothesis. The sugar dissolved faster as the water got warmer. One possible error is that we started the stopwatch late on trial 2." Which part of the lab report is this?
column15: Procedure
column16: Problem
column28: This is the conclusion: it summarizes the analysis, names a possible error, and explains the results. The procedure gives directions, the problem asks the question, and the hypothesis is the prediction made before testing.
column29: Was this written before the experiment, or after the data was analyzed?

column9: Jae is sure his favorite brand of battery lasts the longest. While timing, he stops the stopwatch a little late every time he tests his favorite brand. What is this an example of?
column15: A constant
column16: An independent variable
column28: Bias is an opinion or idea based on beliefs instead of data. Jae's belief changed how he measured, so his data can't be trusted. Scientists must keep bias out of their measurements.
column29: Did Jae's results come from the data, or from what he wanted to happen?

column9: Which of these help make an experiment fair and its results reliable? Select all that apply.
column15: Keep the constants the same in every trial
column16: Leave out data that does not match the hypothesis
column17: Repeat the trials more than once
column18: Change the procedure halfway through to save time
column28: A fair test changes only the independent variable, keeps the constants the same, and repeats trials so the results are reliable. Leaving out data is bias, and changing the procedure midway adds a second variable.
column29: Ask which choices keep the test fair and the data honest.

column9: How is a scientific theory different from a hypothesis?
column14: A theory is a guess, and a hypothesis has been proven.
column15: They mean exactly the same thing.
column16: A theory is an explanation supported by many investigations; a hypothesis is a testable prediction for one investigation.
column17: A hypothesis becomes a law after one experiment.
column28: A hypothesis is a testable prediction made before one experiment. A theory is an explanation built from many observations and investigations, and it can still be modified. Neither one is just a guess.
column29: Which one is built from many investigations, and which one comes before a single test?

column9: Put the steps in order for using a pipette to move a liquid from one container to another.
column14: Release the top so the pipette pulls up the liquid
column15: Press down on the top of the pipette
column16: Squeeze the top to release the liquid into the new container
column17: Put the tip of the pipette into the liquid
column18: Move the pipette to the other container
column28: Press down on the top FIRST, then put the tip in the liquid, so you don't blow bubbles into it. Release the top to pull up liquid, move to the other container, and squeeze the top to release it.
column29: To avoid blowing bubbles into the liquid, think about when the air should come out of the pipette.

column9: Which measurement is recorded with a tool and a unit that match?
column15: Digital scale: 12.5 g
column16: Meter stick: 12.5 mL
column28: A digital scale measures mass in grams (g). A graduated cylinder measures volume in mL, a meter stick measures length in cm or m, and a thermometer measures temperature in °C.
column29: Ask what property each tool measures, then check whether the unit fits that property.

column9: Kai tests whether the type of liquid (water, juice, or soda) affects how fast a sugar cube dissolves. He uses cold water, warm juice, and hot soda. What is the biggest problem with his design?
column14: He should have tested only one liquid.
column15: The temperature also changed, so he can't tell whether the liquid or the temperature caused the difference.
column16: He needs at least ten liquids to have a dependent variable.
column17: Nothing; this is a fair test.
column28: Only the independent variable (type of liquid) should change. Because the temperature changed too, Kai can't tell which one made the sugar dissolve faster. He should use the same temperature for every liquid.
column29: List everything that was different between the three cups.

column9: Volunteers test a new sunscreen. Each person puts the sunscreen on the left arm and nothing on the right arm, then sits in the sun for 1 hour. Then the redness of each arm is measured. What is the right arm in this experiment?
column15: The independent variable
column16: The dependent variable
column28: The right arm gets no sunscreen, so it is the control: the baseline the sunscreen arm is compared to. The independent variable is whether sunscreen is used, and the dependent variable is the redness.
column29: Which arm shows what the sun does with NO treatment?

column9: After one experiment, Group B writes, "Our results prove our hypothesis is true forever." Which response is best?
column14: They are right; one experiment is enough to prove a hypothesis.
column15: They should change their data so it matches the hypothesis even better.
column16: Data can support a hypothesis, but one experiment can't prove it forever; more testing could change the conclusion.
column17: A hypothesis can never be supported by data.
column28: Data can support (or not support) a hypothesis, but science stays open to new evidence. Repeating the experiment and other tests could change the conclusion. Changing data to fit is never allowed.
column29: Can scientists ever be completely sure after a single test?

column9: Jae tests whether the amount of salt (0 g, 10 g, or 20 g) dissolved in 500 mL of water changes the temperature at which the water boils. He uses the same pot and the same burner setting each time. Which choice correctly names the independent variable, the dependent variable, and one constant?
column14: IV: boiling temperature; DV: amount of salt; constant: the pot
column15: IV: amount of salt; DV: 500 mL of water; constant: boiling temperature
column16: IV: burner setting; DV: amount of salt; constant: boiling temperature
column17: IV: amount of salt; DV: boiling temperature; constant: 500 mL of water
column28: Jae chooses the amount of salt (IV) and measures the boiling temperature (DV). The 500 mL of water, the pot, and the burner setting stay the same, so they are constants.
column29: First find what Jae changed on purpose, then what he measured. Everything he kept the same is a constant.

column9: Group E timed three toy cars rolling down the same ramp, three trials each. Car A: 2.1, 2.0, 2.2 s. Car B: 2.9, 3.1, 3.0 s. Car C: 2.5, 2.4, 2.6 s. Which conclusion does the data support?
column14: Car B was the fastest, because its times were the largest.
column15: All three cars were equally fast.
column16: Car C was the fastest, because its times were in the middle.
column17: Car A was the fastest, because it had the shortest average time.
column28: The averages are Car A 2.1 s, Car B 3.0 s, and Car C 2.5 s. A shorter time down the same ramp means a faster car, so Car A was the fastest. A larger time means slower, not faster.
column29: Find each car's average time. Does a faster car take more time or less time?

column9: Leo notices that ice cream seems to melt faster in some bowls than in others. Put his steps in scientific method order.
column14: Makes a graph of the melting times for each bowl
column15: Writes, "If the bowl is metal, then the ice cream will melt fastest, because metal moves heat quickly."
column16: Asks, "How does the bowl material affect how fast ice cream melts?"
column17: Writes that the data supported his prediction and names one possible error
column18: Times scoops of ice cream melting in glass, plastic, and metal bowls
column19: Reads about how heat moves through different materials
column28: State the problem (the question), research (reading about heat), form a hypothesis (If... then... because...), test it (timing the ice cream), analyze the data (the graph), and draw conclusions (supported or not, plus error).
column29: Match each action to a step: problem, research, hypothesis, test, analyze, conclude.

column9: Which student is following ALL of the lab safety rules?
column14: Ben wears his goggles, but takes them off as soon as the experiment ends so he can wash the glassware.
column15: Ana wears goggles, ties back her hair, and stays with her hot plate the whole time it is on.
column16: Cal heats a test tube in a test tube holder with the open end pointed toward his lab partner.
column17: Dee notices a small crack in her beaker but uses it because it is the only clean one.
column28: Ana follows every rule. Goggles stay on through clean up (Ben), the open end of a heated test tube points away from everyone (Cal), and cracked glassware gets reported to the teacher, not used (Dee).
column29: Look for one small rule broken in each of the other three choices.

column9: Ava wants to know whether the temperature of water changes how quickly a drop of food coloring spreads through it. Which plan is a fair test?
column14: Cups of water at 10 °C, 30 °C, and 50 °C holding 100 mL, 200 mL, and 300 mL of water
column15: One cup of 30 °C water, testing red, then blue, then green food coloring
column16: Three cups with 200 mL of water at 10 °C, 30 °C, and 50 °C; one drop of the same food coloring in each, timed, repeated three times
column17: Three cups at 10 °C, 30 °C, and 50 °C, with 1, 2, and 3 drops of food coloring
column28: The fair plan changes only the water temperature, keeps the amount of water and the food coloring the same, and repeats the trials. The plans with different amounts of water or different numbers of drops change a second variable, and the one-cup plan never changes the temperature at all.
column29: For each plan, count how many things change from cup to cup.

column9: Jae gave bean plants 0, 10, 20, or 30 mL of fertilizer. After 3 weeks they were 12 cm, 15 cm, 18 cm, and 11 cm tall. Jae concludes, "More fertilizer always makes plants grow taller." Is his conclusion supported?
column14: No, because height went up from 0 to 20 mL but dropped at 30 mL, so "always" is not supported.
column15: Yes, because the tallest plant got fertilizer.
column16: Yes, because three of the four plants grew taller than 11 cm.
column17: No, because fertilizer had no effect on height at all.
column28: Height went up from 0 mL to 20 mL, then dropped at 30 mL (11 cm, the shortest plant). A conclusion has to fit all of the data, so "always" goes too far. Fertilizer did change the height, so "no effect" is wrong too.
column29: Check every data point. Does the pattern hold all the way to 30 mL?

column9: Group C wrote these directions for their experiment: "Pour some water in a cup. Add some salt. Stir for a while. Measure the temperature." Which changes would make the directions better? Select all that apply.
column14: Give exact amounts, such as 100 mL of water and 5.0 g of salt
column15: Say exactly how long to stir, such as 30 seconds
column16: Name the tools to use, such as a graduated cylinder and a digital scale
column17: Let each person choose how much salt to add
column18: Remove the step about measuring the temperature
column28: A procedure is step-by-step directions that anyone could follow to repeat the experiment. Exact amounts, times, and tools make that possible. Letting each person choose adds a new variable, and removing the measurement step means nothing gets measured.
column29: Could a student in another class follow these directions and do exactly the same thing?
